body.text: When I asked Defense Minister Koizumi Shinjiro how Japan should explain kyohi-ryoku (拒否力) to an international audience, he offered an English rendering: “denial capabilities.”

The exchange took place on November 10 on “SIGNAL,” a political discussion program streamed on YouTube. Earlier that day, the ruling Liberal Democratic Party and its coalition partner, the Japan Innovation Party, had begun working-level talks on revising Japan’s three strategic documents by year’s end. The Defense Ministry’s English summary of Koizumi’s October 28 meeting with U.S. Secretary of War Pete Hegseth uses the fuller phrase “denial defense capabilities.”

Koizumi distinguished between deterrence capabilities and response capabilities. The former help persuade an adversary to forgo an attack; the latter come into play if deterrence fails. Denial is the purpose that connects the two. “Japan will not attack another country on its own initiative,” the defense minister said. He argued that the ability to repel an attack fits Japan’s exclusively defense-oriented policy.

Little of this is new in theory. Deterrence by denial already depends on a credible ability to repel an attack if it occurs. The ability to repel an assault on a Japanese island can deter an adversary from trying to seize it. By making denial a stated priority, Tokyo gives its defense buildup a clear purpose and draws on a vocabulary it shares with Washington.

The U.S. National Defense Strategy released in January calls for a “strong denial defense” along the First Island Chain. The October meeting summary said the two ministers confirmed they would “work to align views” on building this “denial defense.”

A Defense Ministry briefing paper released by November 11 identified four priority capabilities: defense using uncrewed systems, stand-off defense, integrated air and missile defense, and the ability to sustain operations. Sustaining operations under attack requires ammunition stocks, repair capacity, and resilient facilities. With recruitment falling short, Koizumi called for “true integration,” combining overlapping functions while preserving the expertise of the ground, maritime, and air services.

Japan’s Three Non-Nuclear Principles commit it to neither possessing nor producing nuclear weapons and to barring their introduction into Japanese territory. Kyodo News reported that the government was considering retaining all three principles while spelling out an emergency exception to the third in the revised National Security Strategy. The proposal draws on a March 2010 Diet answer by then-Foreign Minister Okada Katsuya. If Japan’s security could not be protected without allowing a temporary port call by a nuclear-armed U.S. vessel, Okada said, the government of the day would have to decide and explain its decision to the public.

Before taking office, Prime Minister Takaichi Sanae argued that the third principle was impractical if Japan relied on U.S. extended deterrence. On October 14, she told a Diet committee the review could address U.S. extended deterrence and Okada’s testimony, leaving the wording open.

On “SIGNAL,” Koizumi said debate on nuclear issues “should be more open” and argued against ruling out options in advance when formulating strategy. He indicated that the final decision rested with the prime minister. Political journalist Tazaki Shiro said that former Prime Minister Kishida Fumio and other LDP lawmakers saw no need to spell out an exception because Okada’s 2010 testimony already gave the government enough flexibility. Kishida has family and political roots in Hiroshima, where the United States dropped an atomic bomb in 1945.

According to Japan’s 2026 defense white paper, China’s DF-26 can reach both Japan and Guam and carry either a conventional or a nuclear warhead. The United States has no equivalent ground-launched intermediate-range nuclear missile, though its guarantee to Japan draws on a broader arsenal, including sea- and air-based nuclear forces. The disparity recalls a question Western Europeans asked during the Cold War: Would Washington risk a nuclear strike on the U.S. homeland to defend an ally facing a regional nuclear threat?

Tokyo and Washington already have guidelines for consultation on extended deterrence. The case for an explicit exception turns on what a port call would add to those arrangements. That question could become more concrete if the United States deploys the nuclear-armed sea-launched cruise missile (SLCM-N) it is developing.

When I raised the stark imbalance in ground-launched intermediate-range nuclear missiles in the region – China fields them, while the United States has none – Koizumi pointed to the October readout, which records an exchange on regional nuclear and missile developments. He went further on air, saying he and Hegseth had also discussed extended deterrence, a term the readout does not use. “The fact that Japan and the United States are discussing these matters is itself an important deterrent,” he said.

Stronger conventional defenses can make it harder for an adversary to achieve a quick military gain under cover of nuclear threats. The case for a port call exception depends on whether it would make the U.S. nuclear umbrella more credible. In the only country to have suffered atomic bombings in war, the government would owe the public a clear explanation of what kind of emergency would justify such a visit.
